title: Book 3 — Thalia, Chapter 413
paragraphs: From Memphis Cambyses came to the city of Saïs with the purpose of doing what he in fact did. For when he had entered the palace of Amasis, he immediately ordered that the corpse of Amasis be brought out of its burial place. When this had been done, he commanded them to scourge it, pluck out its hair, and stab it, and to dishonor it in every other possible way. When they had done this until they were worn out — for the corpse, being embalmed, withstood the violence and did not fall apart in any place — Cambyses ordered it consumed with fire, thereby enjoining a thing not permitted by religion; for the Persians hold fire to be a god. To consume corpses with fire is by no means according to the custom of either people: of the Persians for the reason mentioned, since they say it is not right to give the dead body of a man to a god; while the Egyptians have the established belief that fire is a living wild beast that devours everything it catches, and when sated with the food it dies itself together with what it devours. It is by no means their custom to give the corpse of a man to wild beasts, which is why they embalm it, so that it may not be eaten by worms as it lies in the tomb. Thus Cambyses was ordering them to do what was not permitted by the customs of either people. However, the Egyptians say that it was not Amasis who suffered this outrage, but another Egyptian who was of the same bodily stature as Amasis; the Persians did this outrage to him, thinking they were doing it to Amasis. For they say that Amasis had learned from an oracle what was about to happen concerning himself after his death, and accordingly, to avert the evil threatening to come upon him, he buried the body of this man who was scourged within his own burial chamber near the doors, and enjoined his son to lay his own body as far as possible in the innermost recess of the chamber. These instructions said to have been given by Amasis regarding his burial and the other man are not, in my opinion, ones that were really given at all; I think rather that the Egyptians make this pretense out of pride, with no good ground.
